title: Modern close: saints now
hookLine: holiness keeps showing up in every generation, including this one

lines: FROM A VILLAGE PRIEST IN ARS…
cards: This stretch of the path began in a French village, with a country priest, the Curé of Ars, hearing confessions from morning until night. Since then: a priest among the lepers of Molokai.
Bakhita, sold as a slave and later a Canossian sister. A young Carmelite writing Story of a Soul. A friar in a starvation cell at Auschwitz.
A mother named Gianna. An archbishop at the altar in San Salvador. A pope in an empty square.
A teenager with a website. So, asked plainly: are there saints now?

teach.h: A CALL TO HOLINESS FOR EVERYONE.
teach.b: The Church's own answer starts with the Second Vatican Council, which gave a whole chapter of its teaching on the Church to what it called the universal call to holiness: every baptized person, not only priests and religious, is called to be holy, in a kitchen, an office, a hospital ward.
Saint Paul says it to the Thessalonians, in the Douay-Rheims: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification." Sanctification means being made holy. Not someday, and not only for experts.

Pope Francis wrote a letter on holiness in which he spoke of the saints next door: parents raising their children with love, people working hard to support their families, the sick, elderly religious who keep smiling.
Holiness, he wrote in effect, is found among our neighbors. When the Church canonizes someone, it declares that this person is with God and can be held up as a model.
But the Church does not teach that heaven holds only the canonized. The feast of All Saints honors the whole crowd, named and unnamed.
And some people in this stretch of the path, like Dorothy Day, still have causes open; the Church hasn't finished looking.
In Catholic belief the saints are not gone but alive in God, joined with the living in what the creed calls the communion of saints.

teach.h: THIS IS THE WILL OF GOD, YOUR SANCTIFICATION.
teach.b: Catholics ask for their prayers the way they'd ask a friend. So today's line means two things: the saints of the past are alive in God, and, the Church teaches, new ones are walking around now, mostly unnoticed.

how: Catholics celebrate All Saints' Day for the holy dead known and unknown, ask the saints for their prayers, and in parishes and families tell the stories of holy people they have known.

games.q: you're writing to the whole Church about holiness. where do you tell people to look for it?
o: next door: parents, workers, the sick, the elderly.
games.why: Francis wrote of the saints next door: parents, workers, the sick, elderly religious who keep smiling.

practice: Let someone come to mind whose goodness you've seen up close, a grandparent, a nurse, a friend who keeps showing up: not perfect, just good in a way that stays with you.
Picture one ordinary moment of theirs: their hands at work, a phrase they always say. If you pray, thank God for them by name; if you don't, simply be grateful for them, slowly.

wordCard.voice: Communio sanctorum, Latin for the communion of saints. Holiness showing up in every generation, from the Curé of Ars to a teenager with a website, and in this one too.

orig.note: Latin: the communion of saints, the creed's phrase for the living and the dead joined in God.

carryVoice: Your line: they're still here. Named and unnamed. That's day nine hundred forty-six.
